title: Matcha — AI-Powered Job Aggregator
subtitle: Building a multi-source job search engine that scrapes LinkedIn, Indeed, Naukri, and RemoteOK in parallel, then ranks listings against your profile using heuristic + LLM scoring.
overview: Job searching is broken. You end up with 15 browser tabs open, applying the same filters across 4 different sites, manually comparing roles that don't even use the same terminology. I wanted to build a tool that searches everywhere at once and actually ranks results by how well they match your specific profile.

Matcha is a Python CLI tool that parallel-scrapes multiple job boards (LinkedIn, Indeed, Naukri, RemoteOK), normalizes the results into a unified format, and then scores each listing against your saved profile using a combination of heuristic matching and optional LLM-based semantic analysis.
The result is a ranked, deduplicated list of jobs sorted by relevance — not recency. You save hours of manual searching and get better matches than any single platform's algorithm would show you.
challenge: The Problem: Each job board has different search semantics, different result formats, and different anti-scraping measures. LinkedIn uses internal job IDs, Indeed uses company slugs, Naukri has its own taxonomy, and RemoteOK is API-friendly but limited in scope. Unifying these into a single ranked list requires normalizing wildly different data formats.

Ranking is equally hard. A keyword match isn't enough — 'Platform Engineer' at one company might be 'DevOps Engineer' at another. You need semantic understanding of job descriptions, not just keyword matching.
The tool also needed to work headlessly — no browser automation, no Selenium — to stay lightweight and fast. This meant working with raw HTTP requests and parsing HTML/API responses directly.
solution: I built a modular scraper architecture where each job source is a plugin implementing a standard interface: search(query, filters) → List[JobListing]. Each scraper handles its own authentication, rate limiting, and response parsing, but outputs a normalized JobListing dataclass.

The scoring pipeline runs in two stages. Stage 1 (Heuristic): Fast keyword and tag matching against the user's saved profile — skills match percentage, location compatibility, salary range overlap, experience level fit. This filters the 1000+ raw results down to ~50 candidates in milliseconds.

Stage 2 (LLM Semantic): Optional AI-powered deep matching using a local LLM (via Ollama) or API-based model. This reads the full job description and compares it against the user's experience narrative, understanding context like '3 years of Terraform' matching a requirement for 'IaC experience with HashiCorp tools.'
Results are deduplicated using fuzzy title + company matching (Levenshtein distance), ranked by composite score, and output as structured JSON or a formatted CLI table.

architecture.heading: Plugin Scraper System
content: Each source (LinkedIn, Indeed, Naukri, RemoteOK) is a Python class inheriting from BaseScraper. The base class provides rate limiting, retry logic, user-agent rotation, and output normalization. Source-specific scrapers only implement the parsing logic.
Parallel execution uses asyncio with aiohttp for concurrent HTTP requests. All 4 sources are queried simultaneously, with a total timeout of 10 seconds. Results are merged as they arrive.

architecture.heading: Scoring Pipeline
content: The heuristic scorer computes a weighted score across 5 dimensions: skills match (40%), location fit (20%), salary alignment (20%), experience level (15%), and recency (5%). Weights are configurable per user.

The LLM scorer sends the job description and user profile to a language model with a structured prompt that returns a compatibility score (0–100) with reasoning. This runs on the ~50 heuristic-filtered candidates to keep costs and latency manageable.

timeline.title: Scraper Foundation
timeline.description: Built the BaseScraper class and normalized data model. Implemented RemoteOK scraper first (API-based, easiest). Set up async HTTP infrastructure.

timeline.title: Multi-Source Scrapers
timeline.description: Implemented Indeed and Naukri scrapers. Started LinkedIn scraper (most complex due to anti-scraping). Added parallel execution with asyncio.

timeline.title: Scoring Engine
timeline.description: Built the heuristic scoring pipeline with configurable weights. Added LLM integration via Ollama for semantic matching. Implemented deduplication.

timeline.title: CLI & Polish
timeline.description: Built the CLI interface with Rich for formatted output. Added profile management, saved searches, and export to JSON/CSV. Tested across all 4 sources.

learnings: Normalize early, score late. The biggest engineering challenge was normalizing wildly different data formats from 4 sources. Investing in a clean, unified data model early made the scoring pipeline trivial to build.

Heuristics before LLMs. Running cheap keyword matching first to filter from 1000+ to ~50 candidates made the LLM step both faster and cheaper. The heuristic stage catches 80% of irrelevant results with zero API cost.

Anti-scraping is an arms race. LinkedIn in particular actively blocks scrapers. I used rotating user agents, request throttling, and residential proxy support — but the real lesson is that no scraper is permanent. Design for graceful degradation.

CLI-first is underrated. Building a CLI tool that outputs to terminal, JSON, or CSV means it integrates with everything — pipes, scripts, CI/CD pipelines, other tools. A web UI would have been flashier but less useful.
